<reason>The decisive clash was definitional: the motion compares single-payer to employer-based systems "that tie access to work status." CON's strategy was to defend Germany/Japan/Netherlands as employer-based systems at their best, but every example it offered severs access from work status by law, and CON's own A1 admission that "what German law unties is continuity, not financing" handed PRO its closing line that continuity is access. CON's "unfalsifiable motion" objection was clever but never overcame the motion's own text; CON was effectively defending a comparator outside the proposition. On the residual administrative question (one payer vs. many funds), the exchange was closer: CON landed real hits by forcing PRO to concede private top-up (weakening the bank-balance-rationing point) and by catching PRO's overstated "no enrollment machinery" claim, while PRO's answers on differing kinds of rationing, customer-service-not-clinical-exit, and cherry-picking were adequate. Both sides used the Q/A format properly and grounded claims plausibly; PRO's slight overstatement and clipped turn were minor costs. Overall PRO made the debate easier to decide as written; CON argued a strong but adjacent motion.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's [B2.1]-[B2.2] reframing of CON's Germany/Japan/Netherlands examples as concessions of the motion, then cashed out in [B5.1] by quoting CON's own [A4.1] admission that German law unties "continuity, not financing" — the move that collapsed CON's comparator into PRO's position.</best_rebuttal>
